content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes to:

1. Estimate the mutual information between state and action

2. Use the estimate as regularization, by adding it to the policy and value function objective.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 

The idea of estimating the mutual information between state and action pair and using the estimates to improve policy evaluation and improvement are intuitive.

Weaknesses

The writing is not very clear. I list a few examples below: 

- In the abstract, "Intuitively, mutual information … reflects how a behavior agent reacts to certain environment states during data collection". While this is factually true, I fail to see how this is different from simply estimating the behavior policy. 

- The abstract also writes "equivalent to maximizing the likeli- hood of a one-step improved policy on the offline dataset. In this way, we constrain the policy improvement direction to lie in the data manifold." I do not see how the former leads to the latter, or even what the latter means at all. AFAIK, the data manifold is not defined in the paper at all.

- The introduction writes "Though these methods are effective at alleviating the distributional shift problem of the learning policy, the im- proved policy is unconstrained and might still deviate from the data distribution." This sentence seems self-contradictory. If these methods are effective at alleviating the issue of distribution shift, then how can the learned policy still deviate from the data distribution.

In addition to writing, the paper also has two other weaknesses:

- The paper claims TD3+BC and CQL are special cases, but it is unclear why their method outperforms these methods. The paper claims that their method leads to a better mutual information estimation. But what does "better" mean, and why does that lead to better performance compared to CQL? This is not explained at all.

-  The method does not perform well when learning from uniform data. How about data where the behavior is uniform in some state, but much more constrained in others, which is the more realistic settings? The limitations of the methods seem to be an afterthought that does not receive adequate analysis.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method is novel as far as I know. However, the writing is not clear and too generic. The paper does not release code, so I also do not have high rating as far as reproducibility is concerned.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed idea is novel and intuitive. But the paper writing can be significantly improved, and why the method outperforms baselines deserve more analysis to be more convincing.

content.title: Response to Reviewer SVYL
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. However, we strongly disagree with your comments respectfully.
There were some misunderstandings during the review, and we hope the response can address most of your concerns. If you have any further questions, we can discuss them further.


> **Q1**: On code release

Our code was attached to the supplementary material when submitted. Please take a look. 

> **Q2**: On writing

We are committed to making our paper better understood and delivered. We can revise our paper according to your concrete suggestions. 
However, we do note that all the other three reviewers appreciate that our paper is well-written and easy to follow, as evidenced by the following quotes:

Reviewer **ZgDk** 
> “The writing quality is pretty good overall and I really appreciate the theoretical discourse of this paper. ”

Reviewer **mLZD** 
> "The writing is clear and easy to follow."

Reviewer **aonx**
> "The paper is however well written and easy to follow, with the theoretical derivation for the resulting updates properly derived."

Please help improve the paper if you have concrete suggestions.


 
> **Q3**: For questions on abstract and explanation on why MISA works

We have a detailed derivation and explanation in Sec 4.3 and Equation 14. In summary, with our MISA regularizer, the policy learning step can be understood as a two-stage procedure. In the first stage, It calculates the closed-form optimized policy (which is referred to as the one-step improved policy) based on the current value estimation and policy network. Then, in the second stage, It tries to maximize the likelihood of offline data under this improved policy. In this way, MISA directly restricts the policy improvement direction to avoid OOD problems by keeping in-distribution data have maximal likelihood. 


> **Q4**: For questions on the Introduction

These methods are able to alleviate the problem, but it does not mean the problem is solved perfectly. Moreover, these methods mostly focus on forcing the policy to be close to the behavior policy, the policy improvement direction is not constrained. 


> **Q5**: Not performing well on uniform data?

Could you please explain what you mean by "uniform data"? It would be great if you could point out an offline benchmark or a concrete real-world use case that is focusing on this setting. 

In Sec. 5.4, we discuss the limitation of our methods and show it is not performing well on purely random data.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new framework for handling distribution shift in offline RL, based on a mutual information based regularizer. The mutual information term gives a measure of the data collecting policy's actions on certain states. The regularizer computes a lower bound to the overall policy improvement step and the paper shows how this lower bound can still be useful for leading to overall improvements in offline RL.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The paper proposes a novel regularizer for offline RL and provides intuitions for why such a regularizer might be useful. Existing works have proposed conservative updates to offline RL, but this paper argues the need for such a regularizer. 
	- Mutual information based regularizers have been well studied in online RL literature; so it is interesting to see a use case for it in offline RL; the lower bound is computed using existing approaches in the literature however (lemma 3.1 and 3.2)
	- The main claim of the paper is that this framework can unify two popular offline RL algorithms, namely CQL and TD3+BC. Overall, it leads to the existing algorithms being modified based on equations 5 and 6 and the work shows that this regularizer can lead to a lower bound to the policy improvement step (theorem 4.1)
	- The theoretical justification of this work, along with the derived algorithm, is well explained. However, such techniques are not completely novel and adapts from existing approaches. For example, equation 12 for integrating the regularizer into an offline RL framework is somewhat expected where the additonal term is required based on the approximation of the MI term. 
	- Section 4.4 provides interesting insights for the justification of how the regularizer unifies existing algorithms. 
	- Experiments are primarily done on the D4RL benchmark, and it seems there are marginal improvements due to the addition of the regularizer. However, I am surprised that even in appendix the full result plots are not shown, and it is difficult to judge the actual empirical significance of this work. 
	- Overall, I think the paper is useful in terms of adapting a well known regularizer from online RL into offline RL. However, the resulting approximations for the MI term, and the way it is adapted into offline RL is not completely novel. Even if the algorithm is well derived from existing literature, the empirical significance of the work is not fully clear either.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: - The novelty of this work is somewhat limited, given the approximations for the regularizer have been extensively studied in the past. The paper is however well written and easy to follow, with the theoretical derivation for the resulting updates properly derived. I do have concerns about the reproducibility of the work, since the results are only presented in the form of a table, without actual return plots, and it is not clear to me whether there is a bias variance trade-off due to the addition of this regularizer. Full results not being presented is a major concern for the empirical significance of this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work proposes a novel regularizer based on mutual information. This form of regularizer has been popular in online RL literature, and past works studied approximations to such MI terms. Therefore, the contributions and novelty of this work seems somewhat limited to me. Additionally, the empirical significance of the work is not clear enough. I am willing to re-evaluate my score if the paper clarity can be improved, and experimental significance made clearer.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1028 by Reviewer aonx

content.title: Response to Reviewer aonx
content.comment:
Thanks for your appreciation of the contribution and derivation of our paper. We’d like to address your concerns as below:

> **Q1**: On the novelty aspect

We argue that our proposed method is actually novel. In our paper, we focus on the mutual information between states and actions when an offline dataset is provided. We develop certain methods to estimate this quantity and show that it can be used to supervise policy learning by constraining the policy improvement direction. 

Mutual information (MI) has been explored in online reinforcement learning **in different ways and for different purposes**. To the best of our knowledge, most works use MI to measure the dependency between a state and its subsequent state (i.e., $(s, s')$) in a transition, where our work is measuring MI of $(s, a)$.

In previous works, the MI can be helpful for representation learning [3,5] or intrinsic reward design [1,2]. For example, [1] studies the mutual information between the state and the surrounding state, and uses it as a reward function. Based on the assumption that the agent should take actions that maximize the reduction in uncertainty about the dynamics, [2] defines the MI between the next state distribution and model parameters. Then the information gain is used as a reward signal to encourage exploration. [3] and [5] explore proper ways to measure the MI between states and the next states to boost representation learning in RL, which usually requires a forward model to get the next states. [4] aims at learning a prior policy in replace of the uniform policy to provide a better regularizer than entropy regularization. It is neither able to estimate the MI between states and actions nor able to use it to guide policy learning.  We conclude that prior works have not proposed any similar ideas to our work yet, though all leverage mutual information.

In summary, the technical novelty of our method is two-fold: 1) We are the first to explicitly model and estimate the mutual information between states and actions (MISA) and use it to guide policy learning; 2) We show MISA has a nice property that directly constraint the policy improvement direction as explained in Sec. 4.3 and Equation (14). We will discuss these related works with different techniques in our revised paper. If there is other related literature missing, please let us know and we will revise accordingly. 

[1] Zhao, Rui, et al. "Mutual information state intrinsic control." arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.08107 (2021).  
[2] Houthooft, Rein, et al. "Vime: Variational information maximizing exploration." NeurIPS (2016).  
[3] Kim, Hyoungseok, et al. "Emi: Exploration with mutual information." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.01176 (2018).  
[4] Grau-Moya, Jordi, Felix Leibfried, and Peter Vrancx. "Soft q-learning with mutual-information regularization." ICLR 2018.  
[5] Rakelly, Kate, et al. "Which Mutual-Information Representation Learning Objectives are Sufficient for Control?." NeurIPS 2021

> **Q2**: On the empirical results and reproducibility

Thank you for your suggestion at releasing the training curves. We have updated the curves and plots in the most recent supplementary material, please take a look. We are committed to releasing the complete training curves and logs through wandb.ai platform along with our code. 

For reproducibility, we performed multiple runs of repeated experiments before this submission and the results showed that everything can be reproduced. If you are interested, please use the attached code for a double check. We are absolutely confident on the reproducibility.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a regularization method for constraining policy improvements in offline RL. The proposed regularization is based on a lower bound to the mutual information between states and actions, and attempts to mitigate the issue of distribution shift that arises when the policy is queried on out-of-distribution actions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. The proposed regularization is simple to implement and is well-motivated. It can be easily integrated with most offline RL framework as an additional term in the objective. 

2. The practical algorithm is discussed in detail and implementation details are clearly mentioned. 

3. The ablations and embedding visualizations provide nice intuitions about what MISA is learning empirically. 

Weaknesses

1. Conceptually it is unclear how exactly is MUSA better than prior methods like CQL in mitigating distribution shift. There isn't enough intuition provided regarding this, beyond reference to experimental results and "better mutual information estimation" (in section 4.4) Why exactly should the MI estimation be better?

2. The empirical results do not show strong benefit of MISA over baselines, partly because the hopper, cheetah, walker tasks are almost saturated. For the other tasks in Kitchen, Adroit, and Maze, not all baselines are evaluated, so empirical benefits are unclear.

3. The lower bound result in Theorem 4.1 does not discuss anything about how tight the bound is, and whether the bound still holds in practice (i.e. in the experiments) with several approximations, including function approximations.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mLZD
content.comment:
Thanks for your appreciation of the contribution and novelty of our paper. We’d like to address your concerns as below:

> **Q1**: Conceptually, how MISA is better than previous methods?

It’s well known that offline RL is challenged by the out-of-distribution (OOD) problem. Previous methods try to overcome this problem by making conservative updates or constraining the policy from deviating far from the behavior policy. However, the OOD problem might still exist after one iteration of optimization as the policy improvement direction is not constrained.  With our MISA framework, as shown in Sec. 4.3 and Equation (14), it is equivalent to maximizing the log probability of a one-step improved policy. In other words, MISA actually first calculates the policy improvement direction at each iteration, then force the likelihood of offline data to be maximized after this improvement step is taken.  

> **Q2**: About empirical results

On gym-locomotion tasks, our improvement is actually significant. We beat all baselines on **5 out of the total 9 tasks**. On the other four tasks, MISA is also very close to the best baseline. As a result, MISA surpasses the best overall CQL baseline by **44.4 points** in terms of the total score (MISA 742.9 v.s. CQL 698.5). We argue that this is a clear margin, especially when taking previous SOTAs into consideration. For example, IQL (692.6) is published after CQL but is worse than CQL; **CQL** is **only 13.9 points** better than OneStep RL (684.6). 

For Kitchen, Adroit and AntMaze, we directly quote the results from corresponding papers. These papers may not have full results for every task. We are sorry that re-implementing and reproducing all of them are intractable to us due to time and computation limits. Instead, CQL and IQL are widely accepted as the current state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms, and the experimental results demonstrate MISA's superiority over these two well-established methods. 

> **Q3**: Theorem 4.1

In Equations (8-10) and Appendix A.1, we show that all these bounds are tight and provide the condition under which the corresponding bound is tight. We will make this clearer in the revised version. 

With the assumption that neural networks are universal function approximators, we believe the bound still holds. However, developing theoretical proofs for neural networks is still an open problem not only in our cases but also in other deep learning-based fields. 

We’d appreciate it if the above explanation can address your concerns about our novelty and if you can raise your evaluation of our paper.

The authors motivate their approach step by step and demonstrate how TD3+Behavior cloning and CQL are related to their proposed approach. Finally, the authors provide empirical results relative to key baselines on the D4RL benchmark while also providing ablation studies and analysis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- The authors present a clear buildup to their approach in math and justify each step.
- The authors contextualize their approach pretty well with respect to prior art on a theoretical level.
- The approach gets pretty good performance relative to baselines on the D4RL benchmark. 

Weaknesses: 
- The novelty is not terribly high in comparison to past work on offline RL and mutual information estimation. 
- The introduction of the mutual information regularization in equations 5 and 6 struck me as quite intuitive in nature and not really originating from first principles.

Both: 
- I do really appreciate that the authors clearly highlight limitations of their approach when doing learning from data that is using far from an expert policy. However, on the other hand, it is quite a significant limitation relative to baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing quality is pretty good overall and I really appreciate the theoretical discourse of this paper. The novelty is not very high, but I do appreciate that the authors also clearly present their contribution relative to prior art. The authors have provided their code in the supplemental material.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My biggest concerns about this paper are the relatively low amount of novelty and the fact that the overall motivation is a bit intuitive in nature. However, I lean towards acceptance because I do really appreciate the theoretical discourse and experiments. I feel that in light of this context the authors have provided, the paper is fleshed out enough to make a contribution to the conference, particularly because of its focus on such an important area. 

Update After Author Response: 

I have read through the other reviews and responses to each review. I have kept my score unchanged, but I can't really serve as a strong advocate for this paper either. It is quite outside my area of expertise, so I feel that my confidence is quite low about what the right thing to do here is as I sympathize with all of the points made.

I agree that the novelty is not huge here, but also hear the authors that it is a significant contribution beyond the past literature. However, the results not being too significant could indeed be a potential issue for adoption of this method. Moreover, I think the authors are too quick to discount the importance of not performing well on data from a uniform policy. It is certainly not common for offline RL benchmarks, but if the data compiled by our behavior policy is already "expert" level then offline RL is only improving things at the margins. In typical off-policy RL we start with a uniform policy and while I acknowledge that these are certainly different settings, I think offline RL should be considered harder than off-policy RL (due to lack of access to the underlying behavior policy and lack of access to a simulator during training) and not a strictly easier setting (akin to some slightly more ambitious form of imitation learning).

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZgDk
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback! 

We believe our paper is novel considering the following reasons: 
- You are right that mutual information estimation is widely studied. However, these works are mostly focusing on representation learning and measuring the mutual information between input data and its latent representation. InfoNCE and MINE are two of the most popular MI estimators. They only require a single encoder model. In comparison, measuring the MI between states and actions is much more difficult. Our resulting bounds are also different from InfoNCE and MINE and require an energy function and a policy network. 
- In both online and offline reinforcement learning, we are among the first to explicitly measure the mutual information between states and actions while others might focus on the mutual information between states and states. Based on this formulation, we propose a general offline RL framework that can be integrated with many other RL algorithms. 
- We mathematically show that optimizing our MISA lower bound is equivalently constraining the policy improvement direction during policy learning in Sec.4.3. This provides an insightful explanation of why our framework can work. 
- We show that some existing offline RL algorithms can be understood as special cases of our framework. 

We’d appreciate if the above explanation can address your concerns about our novelty and if you can raise your evaluation of our paper. 

For equations 5 and 6, we just put an overall formulation of our method at the very beginning. Sec.4.2 gives how the MI bound is developed and Sec.4.3 explains why it works.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
(a) Summary: This paper proposes an algorithm for offline RL which attempts to account for the distribution shift problem by constraining policy improvements to satisfy a lower bound on mutual information between states and actions, and empirically evaluates the proposed algorithm.

(b) Strengths: Most reviewers agreed that the paper was very clearly written, with each step well justified.  The authors responsibly highlights that their method performs poorly when the demonstration trajectories are generated using far-from-expert policies such as uniform randomization.

(c) Weaknesses: There were two marginally-positive reviews, but neither were willing to advocate for the paper's acceptance.  Many reviewers were unsure that the novelty of the approach was high enough for acceptance.  The method performs well against baselines, but did not convincingly out-perform other approaches in the literature.  One of the marginally-positive reviewers was especially concerned about the poor performance on uniformly-generated data; they pointed out that a method that only works on data from close-to-expert policies can only eke out marginal improvements almost by definition.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Novelty and empirical performance are really the two main things I'd want to see in a published paper, and the reviewers had serious concerns about both.
